The spectra were aligned by interpolating the second spectrum onto the Raman shift axis of the first. Both signals were then normalized to unit vector length (L2 norm).

args.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Get the two most recent spectra from today
if len(spectra) < 2:
    print("Error: Not enough spectra acquired.")
else:
    s1 = spectra[-2] # X=37
    s2 = spectra[-1] # X=38

    x1, y1 = s1['raman_shift'], s1['intensity']
    x2, y2 = s2['raman_shift'], s2['intensity']

    # To ensure they are on the same axis, we interpolate y2 onto x1's axis
    y2_interp = np.interp(x1, x2, y2)

    # L2 Normalization: v / ||v||
    def normalize(v):
        norm = np.linalg.norm(v)
        return v / norm if norm > 0 else v

    y1_norm = normalize(y1)
    y2_norm = normalize(y2_interp)

    # Cosine Similarity is the dot product of L2-normalized vectors
    cosine_sim = np.dot(y1_norm, y2_norm)

    print(f"Cosine Similarity between X=37 and X=38: {cosine_sim:.4f}")

    # Plotting for visualization
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    plt.plot(x1, y1_norm, label=f"X=37 (normalized)")
    plt.plot(x1, y2_norm, label=f"X=38 (normalized)", alpha=0.7)
    plt.title(f"Normalized Spectra Comparison\nCosine Similarity: {cosine_sim:.4f}")
    plt.xlabel("Raman Shift (cm-1)")
    plt.ylabel("Normalized Intensity")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()
